Follow-up research pass for the same project as before (PIIIX-org/portfolio.me, an agent-run pipeline that forges bespoke personal portfolio sites). A prior deep-research pass covered six areas but only areas 1 (data/info visualization) and 2 (component patterns) survived adversarial verification — 12 and 2 confirmed claims respectively. Areas 3, 4, 5 and 6 produced ZERO surviving claims, because the verification pass demanded peer-reviewed or normative-spec sources, and this material largely does not live there. This pass covers ONLY those four areas, with an explicitly adjusted source policy.

SOURCE POLICY FOR THIS PASS — two tiers, both admissible, but every surviving claim must be tagged with its tier:
- TIER A (normative/measured): W3C/WHATWG specs, platform HIG (Apple, Material, Microsoft Fluent), peer-reviewed HCI research, MDN, official framework docs (View Transitions API, CSS spec text).
- TIER B (practitioner/consensus, admissible but flagged): named practitioners with a track record (e.g. Josh Comeau, Emil Kowalski, Rauno Freiberg, Jhey Tompkins, Sarah Drasner, Val Head, Jakob Nielsen's NN/g, Awwwards/CSS Design Awards jury commentary, newsroom graphics desk blog posts, conference talks with slides/video), and cross-source consensus (the same specific claim independently stated by 2+ unaffiliated named practitioners counts as corroboration even with no peer-reviewed backing). Do NOT admit anonymous SEO listicles, content-mill blogs, or AI-generated roundups — a claim needs an identifiable, credentialed author or organization behind it either way. When verifying a Tier B claim, the adversarial verifier's job is to check whether the source actually says what's claimed and whether it's presented as consensus or as one person's opinion — not to demand it be peer-reviewed research, since it structurally isn't.

THE FOUR AREAS:

3. NEW AND EMERGING VISUAL STYLE MOVEMENTS AND THE ANTI-GENERIC DISCOURSE — named aesthetic/interaction movements in web and product design current as of 2025-2026 (e.g. things like brutalist-minimalism, kinetic typography revival, AI-native/glassy gradients, retro-futurism, anti-design, whatever is actually current — do not assume the answer, find it). For each: its defining mechanics, its characteristic failure mode, the condition under which it's the right choice. ALSO, separately and just as important: what now specifically reads as generic, templated, or "AI-default" in 2025-2026 web design — the tells that mark a site as templated (specific patterns, not vague complaints) — and the named discourse on distinctive versus homogenized web design (design critics, studios, or practitioners who have written specifically about this). This section feeds a real open question about whether documenting current movements at all serves or undermines an anti-template mandate — surface any source that speaks to that tension.

4. MOTION AND INTERACTION IMPLEMENTATION — the View Transitions API (both same-document and cross-document): what it actually does, its current browser support reality, its documented failure modes and gotchas from practitioners who've shipped with it. Shared-element/container transforms (FLIP technique and its named descendants). Disclosure and expansion motion patterns (accordion, drawer, sheet open/close motion specifically — not just their accessibility contract, which is already covered). Chart entrance/transition/morphing animation. Staggering and orchestration patterns (named techniques, not generic "stagger the children"). Scroll-linked and scroll-driven reveals, including the native CSS `animation-timeline`/`scroll()`/`view()` functions versus JS scroll libraries, with real support/performance tradeoffs. Spring/physics-based motion versus duration-and-easing curves: is there real guidance (platform HIG counts as Tier A here) on when each is correct, not just "springs feel nice"?

5. MICRO-INTERACTIONS AND MICRO-ANIMATION — the actual anatomy/principles framework for a micro-interaction (trigger, rules, feedback, loop/mode — this is a named framework by Dan Saffer, verify it precisely rather than assuming). Feedback and affordance signalling for hover/focus/press/drag states specifically. Optimistic UI as a pattern: what it is, when it's right, its failure mode when the optimistic action fails. Haptics and sound as feedback channels for web (not native apps) — is there real guidance or is this mostly unaddressed for web. TIMING NUMBERS SPECIFICALLY: what duration/easing ranges are attributed to actual platform guidance (Material Design's motion duration tokens, Apple HIG's timing guidance) versus what is repeated folklore with no real source (e.g. the ubiquitous "100ms feels instant, 1000ms is the limit before attention wanders" chain — trace this to Jakob Nielsen's actual 1993 "Response Times: The 3 Important Limits" if that's really the source, and report exactly what it says versus what's commonly misquoted).

6. LOADING, PROGRESS AND PERCEIVED PERFORMANCE — skeleton screens versus spinners versus progress bars: is there real evidence (Tier A or strong Tier B) for skeleton screens improving perceived performance over spinners, or is this also folklore? Look specifically for any controlled study, not just practitioner assertion. Streaming/progressive rendering as a perceived-performance technique. Optimistic and predictive loading patterns. Designed preloaders as a deliberate choice (this repo's own doctrine already treats a preloader as a first-class design deliverable, not a spinner — look for what actually justifies that position). Cumulative Layout Shift avoidance techniques — this one IS well-specified (it's a Core Web Vitals metric with a Google-published measurement methodology), so it should be strong Tier A.

DELIVERABLE — same shape as before: landscape per area with concrete named patterns/movements, mechanics, documented failure mode, the condition under which each is right, and citations tagged Tier A or Tier B. Explicitly separate "verified consensus" from "single-source opinion" from "unverifiable folklore" — the folklore-detection is as valuable an output as the confirmed claims, especially for the timing numbers in area 5, since that repo has a HARD rule (§5) that no unsourced claim ships. End with the same kind of repo-mapping section as before: what belongs in STYLES.md (four-part shape: mechanics/Implies/Fails/Right when), what belongs in CRAFT.md (Technique/What it is/Where it earns its place), what's new material, and explicitly answer the open question about whether documenting current style movements helps or hurts an anti-template pipeline.

result.summary: Under the relaxed two-tier policy, this pass recovered solid material for two of the four requested areas and only fragments of the other two. Area 4 (motion/interaction) yielded eight unanimous-or-near-unanimous Tier A claims — all about the View Transitions API specifically (same-doc vs. cross-doc scope and novelty, the static-old/live-new pseudo-element snapshot mechanism that underlies FLIP-style morphing, and the cross-document opt-in/support-matrix/same-origin/progressive-enhancement mechanics) — but zero claims survived on FLIP-descendants outside the VT API, accordion/drawer/sheet motion, chart animation, named staggering techniques, native scroll-driven CSS (`animation-timeline`/`scroll()`/`view()`), or spring-vs-duration HIG guidance. Area 6 (loading/perceived performance) produced strong Tier A material on CLS as a normatively defined, Google-measured Core Web Vitals metric, plus a genuinely contested (not settled) empirical picture on skeleton screens vs. spinners, and NN/g's own practitioner position/thresholds on when to use each loading indicator. Area 5 (micro-interactions) recovered only the precise, verified wording of Nielsen's three response-time thresholds (0.1s/1.0s/10s) and a documented trace of how the popular "100ms instant / 1000ms attention wanders" folklore chain misattributes the 10-second finding to the 1-second mark — nothing survived on Dan Saffer's micro-interaction framework, optimistic UI, or haptics/sound for web. Area 3 (style movements) recovered only neobrutalism as a named, defined movement with a documented failure mode, both from NN/g — the broader anti-generic/templated-tells discourse and named critics on distinctive-vs-homogenized web design produced zero surviving claims even under Tier B, which is itself a data point worth reporting rather than treating as silently absent.

findings.claim: The View Transitions API covers two genuinely distinct use cases — same-document (SPA) transitions via document.startViewTransition() and cross-document (MPA) transitions between real page navigations — and the cross-document capability is not a convenience wrapper: true animated transitions between separate Document objects across a real navigation were literally impossible on the web before this API existed.
findings.evidence: MDN: 'This includes animating between DOM states in a single-page app (SPA), and animating the navigation between documents in a multi-page app (MPA)... Cross-document view transitions ... have historically been impossible.' Chrome for Developers independently restates the same 'historically impossible' framing and confirms no prior API equivalent existed (Chrome 126+ only). Distinct from JS libraries like Turbolinks/Swup/Barba.js, which fake MPA transitions via fetch+DOM-swap within one document rather than a real navigation — not a counterexample. Merges verified claims [0] (3-0) and [1] (2-1).

findings.claim: The API's visual effect is produced by a pseudo-element tree (::view-transition > ::view-transition-group(name) > ::view-transition-image-pair(name) > old/new) in which ::view-transition-old() is a static snapshot/screenshot of the pre-transition state but ::view-transition-new() is a live representation of the post-transition DOM node, not a screenshot — which is why running content such as a playing video continues playing through the transition — and this old/new snapshot-plus-interpolation model is the browser automating the manual FLIP (First-Last-Invert-Play) technique.
findings.evidence: MDN: '::view-transition-old() — A static snapshot of the old view... ::view-transition-new() — A live representation of the new view.' Chrome for Developers: 'the new snapshot is not a screenshot but actually a live representation of the node... the video—sourced from the new snapshot—keeps playing while the view transition is happening.' The FLIP framing is independently corroborated by named practitioners Chris Coyier ('The Shared Element Transition API is FLIPping Cool') and Bramus Van Damme (Google/CSSWG), who both describe the mechanism as the browser automating manual FLIP. Merges verified claims [2] (2-1) and [6] (3-0).

findings.claim: Cross-document view transitions require explicit CSS opt-in on BOTH the departure and destination documents via `@view-transition { navigation: auto; }` (distinct from same-document transitions, which use the JS document.startViewTransition() API); the feature is currently supported in Chrome and Edge from version 126 and Safari from 18.2, but not in Firefox natively as of these sources; it works only for same-origin navigations (identical scheme, host, and port), with no relaxation shipped as of the CSSWG's still-open cross-origin feature request; and because it is a CSS at-rule opt-in, browsers without support simply ignore the unrecognized rule during parsing, making it safe for progressive enhancement with no fallback code required.
findings.evidence: Chrome for Developers: 'both participating pages need to opt-in... In the @view-transition at-rule, set the navigation descriptor to auto'; 'Cross-document view transitions are supported in Chrome from Chrome 126' (Edge 126, Safari 18.2 per WebKit's own blog; Firefox not supported natively, still flag-gated as of 2026); 'limited to same-origin navigations only' (confirmed still-open per CSSWG issue #10364). Chrome's misconceptions blog: 'Browsers that don't support them will ignore the CSS opt-in when parsing stylesheets,' consistent with standard CSS unknown-at-rule tolerance. Merges verified claims [3], [4], [5], [7], all voted 3-0, all Tier A.

findings.claim: Jakob Nielsen's original 1993/2010 three response-time thresholds are precisely 0.1s (feels instantaneous, no special feedback needed, outcome feels user-caused not computer-caused), 1.0s (keeps the user's flow of thought/train of thought seamless/uninterrupted), and 10s (the limit for keeping the user's attention on the task before it wanders/before users start thinking about other things or abandoning). The commonly-repeated folklore chain ('100ms feels instant, 1000ms is the limit before attention wanders') conflates these by moving the 'attention wanders' claim from the 10-second mark, where Nielsen actually places it, down to the 1-second mark.
findings.evidence: NN/g (Nielsen's own byline, restating his 1993 article): '0.1 second is about the limit for having the user feel that the system is reacting instantaneously... 1.0 second is about the limit for the user's flow of thought to stay uninterrupted... 10 seconds is about the limit for keeping the user's attention focused on the dialogue.' A separate NN/g article gives the same figures in Nielsen's own words: '0.1 seconds gives the feeling of instantaneous response... 1 second keeps the user's flow of thought seamless... 10 seconds keeps the user's attention,' with 'after 10 seconds, they start thinking about other things.' Independent secondary sources (e.g. perfplanet.com) confirm the folklore chain genuinely circulates in the conflated ms-based form. Tagged TIER B per this pass's policy (NN/g is the named practitioner source, though it is reproducing Nielsen's own primary claim). Merges verified claims [8], [9], [10], all 3-0.

findings.claim: Whether skeleton screens improve perceived performance over spinners is genuinely contested, not settled folklore-busting in either direction. A Viget (Tier B) controlled study (N=136) found skeleton screens had the WORST average perceived wait time (2.82s) of the three conditions tested, versus spinner (2.41s) and even a blank screen (2.29s), despite identical actual load duration via matched-length GIFs. But a separate, peer-reviewed (Tier A) study (Mejtoft, Långström & Söderström, ECCE'18/ACM) found the OPPOSITE point estimate — skeleton screens scored higher than spinners on perceived speed — while its own authors explicitly state none of the differences reached statistical significance ('cannot show any significant differences in any of the comparisons').
findings.evidence: Viget: 'Average perceived wait time (seconds): Skeleton screen 2.82, Loading spinner 2.41, Blank screen 2.29,' methodology used matched-length animated GIFs to hold actual load time constant. Mejtoft et al. (ACM DOI 10.1145/3232078.3232086, corroborated via Umeå University's DiVA repository): 'The results of this paper cannot show any significant differences in any of the comparisons between the web pages,' despite skeleton screens scoring higher on average and spinner users completing tasks faster. Confidence downgraded to medium specifically because the two admissible sources disagree in direction and neither individual study's headline number should be read as proof; a companion set of overreaching claims drawn from these same two studies were explicitly refuted at 0-3/1-2 vote during verification (see Refuted section) and must not be reintroduced. Merges verified claims [11] and [12], both individually voted 3-0 as accurate reports of what each study itself found — the contested synthesis judgment is the analyst's, not a re-litigation of the individual facts.

findings.claim: NN/g (a named Tier B practitioner source) asserts skeleton screens improve perceived performance by (a) creating an illusion of a shorter wait via suggesting gradual page transition and (b) preventing users from assuming the site is broken — presented as NN/g's own design recommendation/opinion, not as the outcome of an NN/g-run controlled experiment. NN/g separately gives specific, checkable wait-time thresholds for indicator choice: no indicator needed under 1 second; skeleton screens or spinners appropriate for 2–10 seconds; progress bars strongly recommended over 10 seconds — a banding that implicitly follows Nielsen's classic response-time limits, which NN/g cites in the same article's references.
findings.evidence: NN/g: 'Prevents users from assuming the site is broken during loading' / 'Creates an illusion of shorter wait times by suggesting gradual page transition.' Same article: 'If a page takes less than 1 second to load, skeleton screens or spinners aren't necessary'; 'Spinners... are best used when the page takes 2–10 seconds to load... skeleton screens should be used with a wait time that's under 10 seconds'; 'Progress bars are strongly recommended for any page that takes longer than 10 seconds to load,' citing Nielsen's 1993 article in its references. Confidence held at medium (not high) because claim [20]'s wait-time thresholds were voted 2-1 (not unanimous) and its 'supporting quote' in the original source material was flagged by the verifier as a paraphrase/table dressed as a direct quotation rather than verbatim text — a sourcing-hygiene issue worth correcting if reused verbatim in repo docs. Both claims are correctly Tier B (NN/g's own asserted rationale/recommendation, not a controlled NN/g experiment). Merges verified claims [19] (3-0) and [20] (2-1).

findings.claim: Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) is a normatively defined, officially measured Core Web Vitals metric: it is the largest burst of layout shift scores within session windows (shifts <1s apart, capped at a 5s window) across a page's full lifecycle, where each individual layout shift score = impact fraction × distance fraction. Google's published thresholds are 0.1 or less = 'Good,' greater than 0.25 = 'Poor,' with the interval between = 'Needs improvement,' evaluated at the 75th percentile of page visits (sites should have CLS ≤0.1 for at least 75% of visits to qualify as good). Composited transform-based animations (translate/scale/rotate/skew, running on the compositor thread) are specifically exempted from counting toward CLS, whereas animating layout-triggering properties like top/left/box-shadow/box-sizing does count and should be avoided.
findings.evidence: web.dev/cls: 'CLS is a measure of the largest burst of layout shift scores for every unexpected layout shift that occurs during the entire lifecycle of a page' with session windows (<1s gap, 5s max) and formula 'layout shift score = impact fraction * distance fraction'; 'Good CLS values are 0.1 or less, poor values are greater than 0.25, and anything in between needs improvement.' web.dev/optimize-cls: 'sites should strive to have a CLS of 0.1 or less for at least 75% of page visits'; 'Composited animations using translate can't impact other elements, and so don't count toward CLS... Changing the top and left properties also cause layout shifts... Avoid animating using these properties.' Independently corroborated by the WICG Layout Instability API spec repo (transform/opacity animations run on the compositor thread and are excluded from the metric by design). Merges verified claims [13], [14], [15], [16], all voted 3-0, all Tier A official Google Core Web Vitals documentation — this is the strongest-sourced material in the entire pass.

findings.claim: Neobrutalism is a named, currently-active (2025–2026) visual-design movement, defined by NN/g as an evolution of architectural brutalism into digital UI, characterized by high contrast, blocky layouts, bold colors, thick borders, and deliberately 'unpolished' elements. Its documented failure mode: applied without balance or preserved hierarchy, the style's bold high-contrast aesthetic can overwhelm users and actively hinder accessibility (not merely a stylistic risk) — mitigated by retaining hierarchy through size/color-intensity variation and ensuring bold color choices still meet text-contrast standards.
findings.evidence: NN/g: 'Neobrutalism (or neubrutalism), an evolution of traditional brutalism, is a visual-design trend defined by high contrast, blocky layouts, bold colors, thick borders, and "unpolished" elements.' Same article: 'While neobrutalism thrives on bold colors, heavy typography, and sharp contrasts, without balance, it can overwhelm users and hinder accessibility,' with mitigation guidance to 'retain hierarchy through size variation' and ensure 'bold colors must meet text-contrast standards.' Corroborated in substance (not verbatim) by independent practitioner commentary (Medium: 'Brutalism to Neubrutalism: What it means for UX & A11y'). Confidence held at medium: this is a single named Tier B source (NN/g) for both the definition and the failure mode, with only loose secondary corroboration, not independent cross-source consensus in the strict sense the pass's own policy defines for upgrading confidence. Merges verified claims [17] and [18], both voted 3-0.

result.caveats: Coverage is lopsided by design of the verification process, not by researcher choice: Area 4 and the CLS portion of Area 6 are strongly evidenced (mostly unanimous Tier A), while Area 3 and Area 5 are thin — only neobrutalism (area 3) and Nielsen's three thresholds (area 5) survived, out of a much larger requested scope for each. Do not read the absence of surviving claims on Saffer's trigger/rules/feedback/loop-mode framework, optimistic UI and its failure mode on rollback, haptics/sound feedback for web, FLIP-technique named descendants outside the View Transitions API, accordion/drawer/sheet-specific motion mechanics, chart entrance/morph animation, named staggering/orchestration techniques, native scroll-driven CSS (animation-timeline/scroll()/view()) vs. JS scroll-library tradeoffs, spring-vs-duration platform HIG guidance, or the broader generic/templated-tells and distinctive-vs-homogenized-design discourse as evidence those topics lack real sources — it may equally reflect that this research pass's search effort or the adversarial verifier's strictness (even under the relaxed Tier B policy) filtered them out; these should be treated as unresolved gaps requiring another dedicated pass, not as settled non-findings. The skeleton-screens-vs-spinners question is explicitly contested (Viget practitioner study vs. Mejtoft peer-reviewed study, opposite point estimates, and the peer-reviewed study's own authors say neither result is statistically significant) — any downstream doc (e.g. this repo's CRAFT.md) should present this as an open empirical question, not cite either study alone as proof skeleton screens are better or worse than spinners. Browser-support numbers for View Transitions (Chrome/Edge 126, Safari 18.2, Firefox not shipped natively) are time-sensitive as of the 2026-07-27 research date and should be re-verified before being hardcoded into long-lived repo documentation. NN/g content throughout (Nielsen's thresholds restatement, skeleton-screen guidance, neobrutalism) is correctly Tier B by the pass's own policy — practitioner-consensus, not peer-reviewed — and should be tagged as such wherever it lands in repo docs (STYLES.md's four-part shape and CRAFT.md's three-part shape should both carry an explicit Tier A/Tier B tag per the source policy defined for this pass). On the repo-mapping question specifically: the View Transitions API mechanics/mechanism/support-matrix findings map cleanly to CRAFT.md's Technique/What-it-is/Where-it-earns-its-place shape (they are implementation techniques with concrete gotchas, not aesthetic movements); the neobrutalism definition/failure-mode finding maps cleanly to STYLES.md's mechanics/Implies/Fails/Right-when shape (it is exactly a named movement with a documented failure mode); the CLS and Nielsen-threshold findings are cross-cutting reference facts (normative numbers/definitions) that likely belong in whichever doc already holds "hard numbers with sources" rather than forcing them into either four-part or three-part template. On the explicit open question about whether documenting current style movements helps or hurts an anti-template pipeline: no surviving claim in this pass directly addressed that meta-question one way or the other (it was asked for but nothing on it passed verification) — it remains genuinely open and unanswered by the evidence gathered here, not resolved either direction.
openQuestions: Does skeleton-screen usage actually improve or worsen perceived performance versus spinners? The two admissible studies (Viget practitioner N=136, and Mejtoft et al. peer-reviewed ECCE'18) point in opposite directions and neither reaches statistical significance — this needs either a larger/better-powered study or an explicit repo-level decision to treat it as folklore-adjacent rather than settled.

What does the broader 2025-2026 anti-generic/templated-web-design discourse actually say, and who are the named critics/studios writing about distinctive vs. homogenized design? Zero claims survived on this despite it being explicitly requested and despite the relaxed Tier B policy admitting named-practitioner opinion — worth a dedicated follow-up search rather than concluding the discourse doesn't exist.

Is Dan Saffer's trigger/rules/feedback/loop-mode micro-interaction framework findable and verifiable to the precision the brief asked for (verify it precisely rather than assume it), and separately, is there any real web-specific (not native-app) guidance on haptics/sound as feedback channels, or is this genuinely unaddressed in citable sources?

Does documenting current named style movements (like neobrutalism) in STYLES.md actually serve or undermine portfolio.me's anti-template mandate — no surviving source in this pass addressed that meta-question directly; it may require the repo's own maintainers to make a judgment call rather than expecting external sourcing to resolve it.

refuted.claim: Nielsen explicitly reaffirms in this 2010 article that the three limits, originally published in 1993, are unchanged and still apply, and notes they derive from human factors research that was already ~40 years old in 1993 — i.e., not web-specific research at all but general human perception/attention research.

Viget's own controlled UX study (N=136 participants) found that skeleton screens performed worse than both a loading spinner and a blank screen across all measured metrics, directly contradicting the conventional industry belief that skeleton screens reduce perceived wait time.
Skeleton screens scored higher on average than spinners on both perceived speed and perceived ease of navigation in a controlled user study (subjective/self-report measures).

Despite scoring worse on perceived speed/ease, spinners produced FASTER actual task-completion times than skeleton screens for first-time users locating a specific article — perceived performance and actual performance moved in opposite directions.
